latina1.subtitle: {notes} words · both directions, as two cards per word
latina1.tail: THE BEGINNER PASS (November 2026). Start with Latin — Sounds and spelling ({lasounds.notes} cards, days {lasounds.from} to {lasounds.to}), which says how a word is read, what a macron is and how the endings work; this deck follows it on days {from} to {to}, at Folio's default of ten new cards a day, which is five words, since each word is two cards. It now holds {notes} words: {added} were added by hand to the 500 described above. Sixteen are cards no Latin deck had, each built from its Wiktionary entry: seven words of the Core Vocabulary that the build had dropped without a word, because the list and the dictionary name their part of speech differently (nihil, alius, alter, ūllus, uterque, tot, quā); ecce; the three enclitics, which are written on the end of another word (-que, -ne, -ve: estne, vīsne); and five formulas of a first exchange (grātiās agō, quid agis, ut valēs, ita vērō, amābō tē). mālō came down from A2 to stand with volō and nōlō. THE ORDER is no longer the frequency list from the first card. The first {n:quīdam} words are a start written by hand: salvē and valē on day {day:salvē}, yes and no on day {day:minimē}, how are you, thank you and please by day {day:amābō tē}; then the pronouns, the question particles and the enclitics, fourteen prepositions (days {day:in} to {day:apud}), fifteen verbs (days {day:habeō} to {day:sciō}: the irregular ones and one model of each conjugation), the question words, one to ten (days {day:ūnus} and {day:decem}), and one model noun of each declension (puella, servus, bellum, rēx, manus, diēs: days {day:puella} and {day:diēs}). The frequency order follows, with eleven to a thousand and first to third from note {n:ūndecim}, yesterday, today and tomorrow from note {n:heri} and the colours from note {n:albus}. WHAT A CARD SHOWS: under the headword its dictionary entry and, in small capitals, its declension or conjugation. A verb marked suppletive changes its stem (ferō, ferre, tulī, lātum); one marked deponent has passive forms and an active meaning. The English → Latin card asks for the headword: its principal parts or its genitive, and its macrons, are on the back, so say them too. A shorter form that the Core Vocabulary lists is on its word's card (ab: ā, abs; ex: ē; atque: ac; nihil: nīl). THE SPEAKER is an Italian voice reading the word without its macrons: it gives the Church pronunciation (c before e or i as the ch of change, g as in giant, v as in vest, no long vowels), never the classical one the macrons describe (c as in scar, g as in gear, v as the w of west). Latin — Sounds and spelling gives both for every letter. NOT ON ANY CARD, the dictionary having no entry to build one from: nōmen mihi est, which is three A1 cards (nōmen, ego, sum), and salvēte, the greeting to several people (valē's card shows valēte). The Latin shelf, taken in order — Sounds and spelling, A1, A2, B1, B2, C1, the phrases — is {shelfNotes} notes: {shelfDays} days at that pace, {shelfYears} years.

laphrase.subtitle: {notes} phrases · both directions, as two cards per phrase
descSub: The phrases with an article come first, ordered by how often that article was read over two months of 2026, so carpe diem comes long before a phrase of canon law; the rest follow by how often they appear in the Tatoeba corpus and in the classical authors.

They are dealt by reading level, which the end of this description explains; inside a level the phrases with an article come first, ordered by how often that article was read over two months of 2026, so carpe diem comes long before a phrase of canon law, and the rest follow by how often they appear in the Tatoeba corpus and in the classical authors.
Example sentences from Tatoeba come with 177 of the 625 phrases, three apiece for 27, with the phrase picked out in colour.
Example sentences from Tatoeba come with {withEx} of the {notes} phrases, three apiece for {withEx3}, with the phrase picked out in colour.
laphrase.tail: THE BEGINNER PASS (November 2026). THE ORDER is now a reading order: the deck no longer opens with Magna Carta and lingua franca, which English has kept and Latin A1 cannot spell. First come the {byA1} phrases spelled entirely with forms that a card of Latin A1 shows (habeas corpus, anno Domini, cogito, ergo sum, veni, vidi, vici), then the {byA2} that need A2 as well, then {byB1} for B1, {byB2} for B2 and {byC1} for C1; the last {byNone} use a word or a form that no level card shows — names, medieval and legal Latin, rarer forms. A form counts only if a card prints it, in its headword, its dictionary entry or its table. NO MACRONS: the phrases are spelled as the source spells them, and the level decks print the same words with their macrons, so a phrase's long vowels are on the cards of its words. Two phrases left for Latin A1, which now carries them as the dictionary's entries with sentences: quid agis and ita vero. The deck is days {from} to {to} of the shelf, at Folio's default of ten new cards a day, which is five words, since each word is two cards; the first group can be read beside A1.
